hints.hint: For puzzles where agents announce ignorance, first write down exactly what each agent knows. If the setup leaves ambiguous which of two quantities was revealed, that ambiguity is part of every agent's uncertainty: do not case-split externally, assume one reading, and restart. An agent holding x who sees N must keep every partner value legal under either reading (sum/product reveal: N-x and N/x when each is a valid natural number). First move: tabulate candidate own-values x against the partner values surviving for each. "I do not know" means at least two survive, so discard every other x. Apply announcements in order, filtering the set left by the previous one. Trap: roles are fixed, so wondering who holds which number is never a source of doubt; only the two readings of N are. Verify one candidate makes both announcements true and no rival does, then commit to a single value and stop reasoning.

hints.hint: For "all roots lie on one circle" problems, take moduli before hunting roots. FIRST MOVE: from (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, divide by (z-b)^n to get ((z-a)/(z-b))^n = c, then take moduli: |z-a| = k|z-b|. TRAP: k is the n-th ROOT of |c|, not |c| raised to the n-th power; verify k^n = |c| first, since a wrong k gives a self-consistent but wrong circle. Then set z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 terms, divide by their coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius (an Apollonius circle; k=1 gives a line). Check numerically against the ORIGINAL equation, never your derived one: build one explicit root and measure its distance to your center. Report exactly one value, then stop.

hints.hint: Covered area = sum of areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Fix coordinates once, with the shared point at the origin, and never re-derive that setup. Key pruning: only the two edges meeting at the shared point can cut the small square; show the far edges are too distant to matter, so the overlap is a right-angle wedge cut by the small square. Never conclude the small square is wholly covered; the wedge apex sits at its center. Then be numeric, not qualitative: for one angle, find where the two rays exit the square, list the polygon vertices in order, and shoelace it. Repeat for a second angle. If the two values agree, accept that the overlap is angle-independent and do not hunt for a proof; otherwise minimize over the symmetry-reduced range. Trust the shoelace numbers over any closed-form guess, never restart, and once two values agree, report exactly one number and stop reasoning.

hints.hint:
Several hidden degree-n polynomials must jointly hit prescribed values at consecutive integers. Two traps: do NOT difference one polynomial and conclude impossibility, and do NOT assume each polynomial is used once.

Method: write the prescribed value as a function of the INPUT, not the position; for an arithmetic progression over consecutive inputs the target is affine, L(x)=px+q. Fix one polynomial P and set g=P-L. Every input assigned to P is a root of g. Subtracting affine L leaves the leading term untouched, so deg g = n exactly: g is nonzero with at most n roots. The cap is n. Not n+1, which is the interpolation count. Not n-1, which is a finite-difference degree. Multiply that cap over the family for the upper bound, then exhibit a construction giving each polynomial a disjoint block of inputs where it interpolates L. Report one exact integer.

hints.hint:
When unknown points on a fixed curve y=g(x) are tied by a known displacement (u,v), reduce to ONE unknown: let the free vertex be (t, g(t)) and its partner (t+u, g(t)+v), then solve g(t+u) = g(t) + v.

For a logarithmic curve, convert that additive offset to a multiplicative one BEFORE cross-multiplying: log_c(B) - log_c(A) = v means B/A = c^v. Flipping the sign of that power is the dominant failure mode.

If you hit a negative discriminant or impossible identity, the offset is inverted: move c^v to the other side of that one line and re-solve. Do not re-derive confirmed parameters, do not call the configuration impossible, and never estimate from side lengths.

Discard degenerate roots reproducing a given vertex. Finish with shoelace in cyclic order, then report one value and stop.

hints.hint: Describe a configuration by the ordered contents of the truck, gate, and shed rather than by informal move sequences. Legal moves form a small state graph; at each state, attach the actual transition probability, noting that it changes when only one move is available. Each stack is last-in-first-out, so translate the asked-about position into a timing claim: whatever is deposited first sits at the bottom. Then trace only the move sequences that realize that event, multiplying 1/2 per step where two moves were genuinely available, and add those path probabilities. Do not substitute a symmetry claim that each item is equally likely to occupy each position; the induced distribution over orders is not uniform. Report exactly one value per part, then stop.

hints.hint: Interpret the unknown coefficients as weights of a linear functional evaluated at distinct nodes. The vanishing moment conditions say that this functional annihilates a long range of monomials, while the next moment fixes its scale. First move, do it explicitly: absorb the common node factor into new weights w_i = (node i) * a_i, so the vanishing conditions become the moments of exponent 0 upward. A functional killing every polynomial of degree less than the number of nodes is the divided-difference functional, so each w_i equals one scale constant divided by the product of that node's differences from the other nodes; fix the constant from the single nonzero moment. Simplify only the requested endpoint weight and verify the highest prescribed moment. Do not restart from tiny cases; if a small case disagrees, suspect the small case, trust the formula plus that check, then commit to one value and stop reasoning.

hints.hint: Name the unknown whole-number count N of identical units. If each per-unit component amount must be an integer, then N divides every listed component total, so N is a common divisor of all of them: factor them, take their gcd, and use the largest admissible divisor unless a stated layout or grouping condition rules it out. Add all cost components before dividing by N. A percentage markup is multiplicative and commutes with dividing, so fix one order (sum, divide by N, multiply by 1 + rate) and do not re-litigate that ordering. Verify each listed total divided by N is a whole number and that units stay consistent, then report exactly one value and stop.

hints.hint: When the constraint is a commuting identity like p(q(x)) = q(p(x)) with unknown coefficients, do not expand the composition: its degree is the product of the degrees, and drowning in that algebra is the main way these problems are lost. Instead posit the affine link q = -p + b and fix b from the given point values; do not spend budget on the q = p + constant branch, since a nonzero constant shift cannot commute. The identity then collapses to p(-p+b) = -p(p)+b; match the top couple of coefficients to pin p. Expect one leftover free coefficient; verify the requested outputs do not depend on it, then set it to something convenient. Evaluate each requested output through q = -p + b at the needed point rather than re-expanding q term by term - that re-expansion is where sign slips kill otherwise correct work. Recheck the given values once, then report one result and stop.

hints.hint: First move: for the two smallest sizes, write positions 0..N-1 as an explicit list and rewrite the entire list after each stage k=0,1,...,n-1 in order; that is one operation. After every stage the list must still contain each label exactly once; if two labels land in one slot your bookkeeping is broken, so redo that stage by physically swapping the two blocks. Reapply it and track the orbit of a single label until it repeats. That cycle length is your candidate order. Then write positions in binary and express the whole operation as one map on bit strings (which bits flip, which rotate), and verify it reproduces both explicit traces. Trap: never accept a shortcut claim about the net effect unless it matches your trace; if a formula and a trace disagree, trust the trace. Once two sizes agree, stop exploring, never restart the analysis, and report exactly one closed form in n, then stop.
